title: The Divine Comedy
author: Dante Alighieri
openingText: In the middle of the journey of our life I came to myself within a dark wood where the straight way was lost. Ah, how hard a thing it is to tell what a wild, and rough, and stubborn wood this was, which in my thought renews the fear! So bitter is it that scarcely more is death: but to treat of the good that I there found, I will relate the other things I discerned.
about: Dante is 35 — midway through life — and lost in a dark wood. A dead Roman poet arrives to guide him through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. The journey takes one week. The poem took twelve years to write and contains the entire medieval cosmos, plus Dante's personal enemies, alphabetically arranged in torment.

angleCards.title: The audacity of placing your enemies in Hell.
angleCards.text: Dante condemned real people — popes, politicians, rivals — to specific torments while they were still alive. I want to track who he put where and why, and ask what it means to claim God's judgement as your literary device.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Divine Comedy paying attention to the political audacity — Dante placing living enemies in Hell by name — and what it reveals about medieval justice, personal vendetta, and the claim to divine authority.

angleCards.title: Beatrice as the force that moves everything.
angleCards.text: She is the woman who sends Virgil to rescue Dante in the dark wood. She is the guide through Paradise. She is, for Dante, the face of divine love. I want to understand why a real woman he barely knew becomes the universe's organising principle.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Beatrice as the organising principle of the whole poem — what she represents, why Dante structures the entire cosmos around divine love, and whether that framework still makes sense.

angleCards.title: The Inferno as a map of the self.
angleCards.text: The poem begins with Dante lost in a dark wood at midlife. Every circle of Hell he descends through is a category of human failure. I want to read the descent as interior — what it says about what Dante feared, regretted, and was tempted by.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the descent through Hell as psychological — a map of human failure and self-deception — and ask what Dante thought he was afraid of in himself.

angleCards.title: The architecture of moral philosophy.
angleCards.text: Every location in the Comedy is designed — sins punished by contrapasso (the punishment mirrors the crime), virtues rewarded by proximity to God. I want to follow the logic of that structure and understand the complete moral system Dante built into the geography of the afterlife.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the architecture of the afterlife — how Dante's moral philosophy is built into the structure of Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise — and what that system reveals about medieval Christian ethics.

cast.name: Dante
cast.description: The protagonist and narrator — a 35-year-old Florentine poet in spiritual crisis, guided through the afterlife to find his way back. The poem is structured as his journey, but it is also a self-portrait of the most ambitious kind: the man who mapped the moral universe.

cast.name: Virgil
cast.description: The Roman poet who guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory. He represents human reason — wise, noble, and ultimately insufficient. He cannot enter Paradise because he lived before Christ. The limit of reason is the point where faith must take over.

cast.name: Beatrice
cast.description: A Florentine woman Dante loved from childhood who died at 24. In the poem she is the force that initiates the whole journey — it is her concern for Dante that sends Virgil — and she guides him through Paradise. She is theology made personal.

cast.name: Francesca da Rimini
cast.description: A noblewoman condemned to Hell's second circle for adultery, who tells her story so beautifully that Dante weeps and faints. She is the Inferno's most famous encounter — and Dante's most honest admission that Hell and sympathy can coexist.

cast.name: Ulysses
cast.description: Homer's Odysseus, in Hell for fraud — but Dante gives him a final voyage no ancient source describes: sailing past the Pillars of Hercules into the unknown and drowning within sight of Purgatory. His punishment is for going too far. Dante is fascinated and does not fully condemn him.

cast.name: St. Bernard
cast.description: The medieval mystic who takes over from Beatrice in the final cantos of Paradise, guiding Dante toward the direct vision of God. He represents contemplative prayer — the mode of knowing that lies beyond reason and even beyond love as normally understood.
